text: A daughter of Hokusai by his second wife, Kotome, Ōi was an accomplished painter who also worked as a production assistant to her father. Her birth and death dates are not known, although it is believed that she was born in 1800 and died around 1866. Her works include Three Women Playing Musical Instruments and Operating on Guan Yu's Arm. She is counted among the ukiyo-e artists of the Edo period.

Blondeel did a lot besides painting: in Bruges he worked as an architect, city planner, surveyor and cartographer, and he designed sculptures and jewelry as well as woven wall hangings. He came from Poperinge and joined the Guild of Saint Luke in 1519. He trained Pieter Pourbus, who married his daughter Anna in 1543 and took over his atelier. He painted mostly religious works commissioned by local churches. In 1550 he and Jan van Scorel were commissioned to restore a celebrated work by Jan van Eyck.

Kilburn was for nearly twenty years the portraitist of choice in New York City, and he is said to have been the first portraitist there. One source says he was a Moravian of Danish birth. He arrived in New York from London in May 1754 on the brig Maria and immediately announced his presence in two newspapers, the New York Gazette and the New York Weekly. His first advertisement ran on 13 May.

Delaporte was educated in Amiens and became a student of Jean-Baptiste Regnault in 1824. An eye disease forced him to give up painting, so he turned to writing. His plays were presented on the most important Parisian stages of the century, among them the Théâtre des Folies-Dramatiques, the Théâtre du Palais-Royal and the Théâtre des Variétés. He also made many lithographs and illustrations for newspapers, and he drew political caricatures.

Porpora specialised in still lifes, mostly of flowers, and worked mainly in Naples. He is documented as a pupil of Giacomo Recco and is said to have worked under Aniello Falcone. From 1656 to 1658 he belonged to the Accademia di San Luca in Rome, where Netherlandish still-life painters seem to have influenced him. His pupils included Giovan Battista Ruoppolo and Onofrio Loth. Some of his still lifes show snakes, frogs and fly agarics among thistles and wild roses.

Bell was articled at an early age to John Beugo, the friend of Robert Burns, and while in his studio he also attended classes at the Trustees' Academy under Sir William Allan. After leaving Beugo he engraved a series of Scottish views and a considerable number of vignette portraits. His son, Robert Purves Bell, became a painter of figure subjects. Bell was born and died in Edinburgh.

Recruited in Rome by the Spanish ambassador to the Holy See and commended to Philip II, Cincinato, who was born in Florence, became active in Spain after 1567. He painted for the Escorial. An altarpiece of the Circumcision in the Jesuits' church at Cuenca was his best-known work. Patricio Caxes of Arezzo went with him and painted much in the Pardo. His two sons, Diego and Francisco Romulo, were painters in Spain.

Bridgford moved with his family to Ireland in 1817 and first exhibited at the Royal Hibernian Academy at fifteen. In 1834 he went to London to work as a portrait painter, and he exhibited regularly at the Royal Academy while he was there. He returned to Dublin in 1844. He produced portraits, paintings and lithographs in England and Ireland. Many of his pencil portraits show scientific members of University College London.

A Scottish engraver working in London, Elder was employed mainly by booksellers. He engraved many portraits as frontispieces, mostly copied from older engravings, but he was an expert at engraving writing. He also engraved the plates in John Savage's edition of Richard Knolles and Paul Rycaut's History of the Turks, published in 1701. He engraved his own portrait twice, once in a fur cap and once in a wig.

Kien's father was one of the most important members of the Yanagisawa clan, whose princely seat was Kōriyama Castle. As a child in Edo he developed an interest in painting at the age of nine. He began training with artists of the Kanō school but became a disciple of a painter who practised the Nagasaki-e style of woodcut art. Later he studied nanga painting under Gion Nankai. His art names included Chikkei and Gyokkei.

Cobergher is chiefly remembered today as the man responsible for draining the Moëres on the Franco-Belgian border. He is also considered one of the fathers of the Flemish Baroque style of architecture in the Southern Netherlands. As a painter he faded from view. He was born in Antwerp, probably in 1560, a natural child of Wenceslas Coeberger and Catharina Raems. He worked as an architect, engineer, antiquarian, numismatist and economist as well.

Wu Changshuo, born Wu Junqing, worked as a calligrapher and painter and also as a seal artist in the late Qing period. He was born in Anji County, in Zhejiang Province, and grew up in a scholarly family. He is best known for his painting. He excelled at painting flowers, particularly plum blossoms and peonies. His works are characterized by bold, vivid colors and powerful brushstrokes.

Carpelan came from a Finnish noble family and served as a Swedish officer, working as a draftsman and surveyor. With Johannes Flintoe and another colleague, he was one of the first to survey and describe the interior of Norway. He covered Telemark in particular. When Sweden had to cede Finland to Russia in 1809, he stayed in the Swedish Army, and he took part in the construction of the Göta Canal. His Rjukan Falls in Telemark is among his drawings.

Vaszary came from a prominent Catholic family in Kaposvár, and his uncle Kolos Ferenc Vaszary was the Archbishop of Esztergom. He began his art studies under János Greguss, and in 1887 he went to Munich to study with Gabriel von Hackl and Ludwig von Löfftz. After seeing an exhibition of paintings by Jules Bastien-Lepage he moved to Paris in 1899 and enrolled at the Académie Julian. Later he became involved with Simon Hollósy and the artists' colony in Nagybánya.

Born in The Hague, Borman may have been related to the landscape painter Abraham Borman. He worked in Leiden for several years in the 1650s and became a member of the Leiden Guild of St Luke. In 1659 he moved to Amsterdam, where he signed in as a citizen and declared that he was a painter in The Hague. He is known for fruit and flower still lifes.

Rembrandt never went abroad. Italian Old Masters still influenced him. His roughly 100 self-portraits, more than 40 of them paintings, form an intimate autobiography. He was the ninth child of a miller and a baker's daughter in Leiden. After a short time at Leiden University he turned to painting and shared a studio with Jan Lievens. At the end of 1631 he moved to Amsterdam, and in 1634 he married Saskia van Uylenburgh.

Born Eliseo D'Angelo in Italy, Visconti became a Brazilian painter, cartoonist and teacher. He is considered one of the very few Impressionist painters of Brazil and the initiator of Art Nouveau there. In 1884 he entered the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios in Rio de Janeiro, where he studied under Victor Meirelles. At the same time he studied at Brazil's Imperial Academy of Fine Arts, under Henrique Bernardelli and Rodolfo Amoedo, among others.

Passmore painted fruit for the US Department of Agriculture as a botanical illustrator. She rose to lead the department's staff artists and became the most prolific of the group, contributing one-fifth of the 7500 paintings in the Pomological Watercolor Collection. She has been called the best of the early USDA artists. She was born in Delaware County, Pennsylvania, the fifth and last child of a farmer.

Goltzius has been described as the leading Dutch engraver of the early Baroque, or Northern Mannerism. According to Hyatt Mayor, he was the last professional engraver who drew with the authority of a good painter and the last who invented many pictures for others to copy. He was born near Viersen and became a Dutch printmaker, draftsman and painter. In the middle of his life he also began to produce paintings. His The Fall of Man dates from 1616.

Steadman worked for the US Department of Agriculture as a botanical illustrator and a wax fruit modeler. He developed a patented method of strengthening wax fruit with plaster on the interior. He was born in Portland, Maine, and his parents separated when he was young. He studied art at the School of the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston and at the Cowles Art School in the same city.

The Van de Passe family was a dynasty of Dutch engravers started by Crispijn the Elder, comparable to the Wierix family and the Sadelers, though mostly working at a more commercial level. Most of their engravings were portraits and book title-pages, with relatively few grand narrative subjects. Their style is very similar, so the family members are hard to tell apart without a signature, a date or evidence of location. Many of them produced their own designs and left drawings. Crispijn the Elder came from Arnemuiden.

Doré is best known for his prolific output of wood-engravings illustrating classic literature, above all the Vulgate Bible and Dante's Divine Comedy. These had great international success. His role was normally as the designer only. At the height of his career some 40 block-cutters were employed to cut his drawings onto the wooden printing blocks, and they usually signed the image too. He created more than 10,000 illustrations.

Lear is known mostly for his literary nonsense in poetry and prose, especially the limericks that he popularised but never called by that name. As an artist he worked in three areas. He was a draughtsman who illustrated birds and animals, he made coloured drawings during his journeys and reworked them later, sometimes as plates for his travel books, and he was a minor illustrator of Alfred, Lord Tennyson's poems. He was also a musician.

Newton painted watercolors of fruit as a botanical illustrator for the US Department of Agriculture. She is the second-most prolific contributor to the department's Pomological Watercolor Collection, with roughly one-sixth of its 7600 paintings. She was the granddaughter of Isaac Newton, the first commissioner of the USDA, who died when she was a child. Her colleague Royal Charles Steadman later painted a portrait of her.

Signac's parents wanted him to study architecture, but he preferred to draw the Seine. An 1880 exhibition of Claude Monet's work affected him particularly. In 1884 he met Monet and Georges Seurat, and he was struck by Seurat's systematic working methods. He helped Seurat develop pointillism. A keen sailor, he is best known for his seascapes and views of ports and rivers.

Arnold worked for the US Department of Agriculture for more than thirty-five years, painting watercolors of a wide variety of fruits. She studied art in New York and began her career with the department in 1904. She belonged to a select group of illustrators that also included Deborah Griscom Passmore, Amanda Newton, Elsie Lower, Royal Charles Steadman and Marion Shull. She is one of the three most prolific artists in the Pomological Watercolor Collection. Very little else is known about her.

Wyspiański wrote symbolic national dramas in keeping with the aims of the Young Poland movement, and he was a patriotic writer. He was also a painter and poet, and he designed interiors and furniture. He combined modernism with traditional Polish folk and Romantic themes. He became known unofficially as a fourth Polish bard, after Adam Mickiewicz, Juliusz Słowacki and Zygmunt Krasiński. He worked in many fields in Poland under the foreign partitions.

Waud made his name with the sketches he drew as an artist correspondent during the American Civil War. He was born and raised in Hackney, London, the eldest son of Alfred Waud Sr. and Mary Fitz-John. He was christened Alfred Robert, but while living in the United States he used Rudolph as a middle name. He had four younger siblings. He worked as an artist and illustrator in America.

A leading member of the Vienna Secession movement of architecture, founded in 1897, Wagner also belonged to the broader Art Nouveau movement. Many of his works are in his native Vienna and illustrate the rapid evolution of architecture there. His early works were inspired by classical architecture. By the mid-1890s he had designed several buildings in what became known as the Vienna Secession style. Beginning in 1898, with his designs for Vienna Metro stations, his style became floral.

Everdingen came from Alkmaar, the son of a government clerk. According to Houbraken, he and his older brothers, the painters Jan and Caesar van Everdingen, were taught by Roelandt Savery in Utrecht. In 1645 he moved to Haarlem and studied under Pieter de Molijn, and in February of that year he married Janneke Cornelisdr. He finally settled in Amsterdam about 1657 and died there. He made etchings and mezzotints as well as paintings.

The most fashionable artist of his day, Romney painted many leading society figures, including his artistic muse Emma Hamilton, the mistress of Lord Nelson. He was the third of eleven children of a cabinet maker, born in Dalton-in-Furness in Lancashire. As a schoolboy he seems to have been indifferent, and he was withdrawn at eleven and apprenticed to his father's business instead. He grew up in a cottage called High Cocken.

Thorburn specialised in wildlife and painted mostly in watercolour. He explored Scotland to sketch birds in the wild, and his favourite haunt was the Forest of Gaick near Kingussie. His images of British wildlife were set in front of dramatic backgrounds and were widely reproduced. He was the fifth son of Robert Thorburn, portrait miniaturist to Queen Victoria. He painted a Peacock.

Besnard studied at the École des Beaux-Arts and with Jean Bremond, and Alexandre Cabanel influenced him. He won the Prix de Rome in 1874 with Death of Timophanes. In 1879 he married the sculptor Charlotte Dubray, and three of their four children became artists. Until about 1880 he followed the academic tradition, but then he broke away and devoted himself to colour and light as the Impressionists conceived them.

Witsen came from the wealthy Witsen family of Amsterdam, which went back to the governing families of the Dutch Golden Age. He studied at academies in Amsterdam and Antwerp and founded the Nederlandse Etsclub, the Dutch Etching Club. He belonged to the Tachtigers, young artists who proclaimed art for art's sake, and he supported their literary magazine De Nieuwe Gids with money and with articles written under a pseudonym. On visits to London he got to know the paintings of James McNeill Whistler. He worked as a painter and photographer.

Mondrian started out as a primary school teacher who also painted, and most of his early work is naturalistic or Impressionistic landscapes with windmills and rivers. His father was a qualified drawing teacher, and he often painted along the river Gein with his uncle Frits. He moved from the Netherlands to Paris in 1912 and removed an a from the Dutch spelling of his name, Mondriaan. He co-founded De Stijl with Theo van Doesburg. Over time he reduced his work to horizontal and vertical lines and a handful of colors.

A Franciscan friar, Coronelli became one of the leading cartographers of the Baroque period, known above all for his atlases and globes. At ten he was sent to Ravenna to be apprenticed to a woodcut engraver. A little before 1678 he began working as a geographer and was commissioned to make a set of terrestrial and celestial globes for Ranuccio II Farnese, Duke of Parma. Each globe was five feet across and so impressed the duke that he made Coronelli his theologian. He returned to Venice in 1705 and began his Atlante Veneto.

The eldest of six children in Bern, Hodler had lost his father and two younger brothers to tuberculosis by the time he was eight. His father had made a meager living as a carpenter, and his mother came from a peasant family. His early works were portraits, landscapes and genre paintings in a realistic style. Later he adopted a personal form of Symbolism that he called parallelism.

The son of a Jewish banker, Liebermann studied art in Weimar, Paris and the Netherlands. After living and working in Munich for some time he returned to Berlin in 1884, where he stayed for the rest of his life. He became one of the leading proponents of Impressionism in Germany and continental Europe. He also assembled an important collection of French Impressionist works. Later he chose scenes of the bourgeoisie and parts of his garden near Lake Wannsee as motifs.

Born Julius Mordecai Pincas, Pascin was a Bulgarian artist of the School of Paris, nicknamed the Prince of Montparnasse. He was educated in Vienna and Munich and travelled in the United States, spending most of his time in the South. He later became an American citizen. His most frequent subject was women, in casual poses, usually nude or partly dressed.

The third son of a sporting artist, Samuel Alken, Henry Alken had two brothers who were artists, George and Samuel Alken the Younger. He was chiefly known as a caricaturist and illustrator of sporting subjects and coaching scenes. His most prolific period of painting and drawing came between 1816 and 1831. He was born in Soho, and in 1789 the family moved to Francis Street East near Bedford Square.

Schutt painted fruit as a botanical illustrator for the US Department of Agriculture, and her work is now part of the Pomological Watercolor Collection in the National Agricultural Library. She was born on the Oak Grove estate in Arlington, Virginia. Her father, Francis Granger Schutt, was a merchant of Dutch descent. She was one of seven children, with two brothers and four sisters, and the family grew up in what is now Cherrydale.

Known for his iris and daylily cultivars and for his botanical illustrations, Shull worked as an American botanist. His family produced several prominent biologists. His brother Charles Albert Shull was a plant physiologist at the University of Chicago, and George Harrison Shull, a geneticist at Princeton, pioneered work on heterosis in maize. Another brother, Aaron Franklin Shull, was a zoologist at the University of Michigan.

Spitzweg painted genre subjects, and he is considered one of the most important artists of the Biedermeier era. He was born in Munich, the second of three sons. His mother was the daughter of a wealthy fruit wholesaler, and the family's stately property at Neuhauser Straße 14 later gave him financial independence through his inheritance. The Poet in his Shirt at his Writing Desk is among his pictures.

Dordrecht was where Cuyp was born and died, the most famous of a family of painters. He learned from his father, Jacob Gerritszoon Cuyp, while his uncle Benjamin and grandfather Gerrit designed cartoons for stained glass. He is especially known for large views of Dutch riverside scenes in golden early morning or late afternoon light. He inherited a considerable fortune. He is known as the Dutch equivalent of Claude Lorrain.

A pupil of Martin Schongauer in Colmar, Burgkmair lost his master when Schongauer died in 1491, before he had completed the normal period of training. He then worked in Augsburg, where he became a master and in 1498 opened his own workshop. He certainly visited Italy in 1507, and the trip greatly influenced his style. He was the son of the painter Thomas Burgkmair, and his own son, Hans the Younger, became a painter too.

The Paris Louvre was where Vernet was born, because his parents were staying there during the French Revolution. His father, Carle Vernet, was a painter, and so was his grandfather Claude-Joseph Vernet. He quickly developed a disdain for the high-minded seriousness of academic French art, which was marked by Classicism, and he decided to paint subjects taken mostly from contemporary life. He painted battles, portraits and Orientalist subjects.

A native of Wilmington in Delaware, Pyle spent the last year of his life in Florence, Italy. In 1894 he began teaching illustration at the Drexel Institute, where his students included Violet Oakley, Maxfield Parrish and Jessie Willcox Smith. After 1900 he founded his own school, the Howard Pyle School of Illustration Art. The scholar Henry Pitz later used the term Brandywine School for this illustration tradition. Pyle wrote and illustrated mainly books for young people.

A leading exponent of history painting in the nineteenth century, Matejko painted nodal events from Polish history. His large oil paintings include Stańczyk, Rejtan, Union of Lublin and Battle of Grunwald. He also made numerous portraits and a gallery of Polish monarchs in book form, and he painted murals in St. Mary's Basilica in Kraków. Maurycy Gottlieb, Franciszek Żmurko and Franz Streitt all studied under him.

Watts was named George Frederic after Handel, because he was born in Marylebone on Handel's birthday. His father was a poor piano-maker, and Watts was the son of his second wife. Delicate in health, he later became famous for allegorical works such as Hope and Love and Life. They were meant to form part of an epic symbolic cycle called the House of Life. He also sculpted.

The Sadelers were the largest and probably the most successful dynasty of Flemish engravers. They were dominant in Northern European printmaking in the later 16th and 17th centuries, as both artists and publishers. At least ten Sadelers worked as engravers, in the Spanish Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Bohemia and Austria. Their style is very similar, so their work is often hard to tell apart without a signature or date. Many of their best prints were reproductions.

Kandinsky is generally credited as one of the pioneers of abstraction in Western art. He was born in Moscow. He began his painting studies, life-drawing, sketching and anatomy, only at the age of thirty. In 1896 he settled in Munich, first at Anton Ažbe's private school and then at the Academy of Fine Arts. There he was first the teacher and then the partner of the German artist Gabriele Münter. He returned to Moscow in 1914 after the outbreak of the First World War.

Baron László Mednyánszky came from an aristocratic background, but he spent most of his life moving around Europe working as an artist. He was also a philosopher, and he is considered one of the most enigmatic figures in the history of Hungarian art. He spent considerable periods in seclusion. Yet he mingled with people across society, in the aristocracy, the art world, the peasantry and the army, and many of them became subjects of his paintings.

An English book illustrator, Rackham is recognised as one of the leading figures of the Golden Age of British book illustration. His work is noted for strong pen and ink drawings combined with watercolour, a technique he developed because of his background as a journalistic illustrator. His 51 colour pieces for Rip Van Winkle were a turning point in book production, since colour-separated printing meant they could be reproduced accurately. That was new.

Wouwerman painted hunting, landscape and battle scenes, and he was a prolific artist of the Dutch Golden Age. He was baptized in 1619 and joined the Haarlem Guild of St Luke. Haarlem was his home town. His pictures were in demand during his lifetime and even more sought after in the 18th century. Princely art collections across Europe hold his work.
